questions.question: Systems are usefully divided in three by their response-time expectations. Which three?

options.text: Services, batch processing systems, and stream processing systems
OLTP, OLAP, and hybrid transactional-analytical systems
Synchronous, asynchronous, and partially synchronous systems
Leader-based, multi-leader, and leaderless systems

questions.explanation: A service waits on a user and is judged by response time; a batch job runs over bounded input and is judged by throughput; a stream processor consumes unbounded input shortly after events occur.

questions.question: Which interaction style is used by databases, caches, search indexes, and web servers?

options.text: Request-response processing
Batch jobs scheduled nightly, as in data warehouses
Streams of events processed continuously
Peer-to-peer gossip between nodes

questions.explanation: Request-response systems receive a bounded request or query and eventually return a result. Databases, caches, search indexes, and web servers commonly use this interaction style; batch systems instead consume a bounded dataset without a user waiting on each record.

questions.question: What can generally be assumed about a request in an online system?

options.text: That a human triggers it and is waiting for the response
That it is triggered by another machine and nobody is waiting
That it is idempotent and can be retried freely
That it touches only one partition

questions.explanation: A waiting human is what makes response time the governing metric.

questions.question: Match each processing style to its primary performance measure. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Services (online systems) wait for a request or instruction to arrive and try to handle it as quickly as possible, sending a response back; response time is usually the primary measure of performance, and availability is often very important — if the client can't reach the service, the user will probably get an error message

Batch processing systems (offline systems) take a large amount of input data, run a job to process it, and produce some output data; the primary performance measure is usually throughput — the time it takes to crunch through an input dataset of a certain size

Stream processing systems (near-real-time systems) consume inputs and produce outputs rather than responding to requests; a stream job operates on events shortly after they happen, which allows lower latency than the equivalent batch systems
All three of them are measured primarily by their availability rather than by throughput or latency, because a system that is reachable is by definition keeping up with its workload

questions.explanation: Online services optimize the delay perceived by a waiting requester, batch systems optimize records or bytes processed per unit time, and stream processors optimize how quickly an event affects an output.

optionExplanations.a: An online service handles one waiting client's request, so perceived response time and reachability dominate. High aggregate throughput does not compensate for a user-facing request that stalls.
optionExplanations.b: A batch job consumes a bounded dataset without a person awaiting each record, making total throughput the natural measure. The goal is to finish a given volume efficiently.
optionExplanations.c: A stream processor continuously turns newly arriving events into outputs, so event-to-result latency is central. Unlike batch processing, it does not wait for a bounded input to end.
optionExplanations.d: Availability only says requests can reach a system; it does not show that a batch job has good throughput or a stream is keeping up. Each processing style has a different primary performance concern.

questions.question: How long do batch jobs take?

options.text: They take minutes to days, with no user waiting for the result
Jobs take seconds and are triggered by user requests
Jobs take hours and are triggered by incoming events
Jobs run continuously with no scheduling

questions.explanation: Batch jobs consume a finite dataset without a user waiting on each record. They commonly run for minutes to days under a periodic scheduler and publish their result when the whole job finishes.

questions.question: On what property does the line between stream and batch processing fall?

options.text: On the boundedness of the input
On latency alone, which is the defining difference
On whether the data is in HDFS or in a queue
On whether the job is scheduled or continuous

questions.explanation: Boundedness, not latency, is the structural distinction. A batch job can eventually observe the end of its input, while a stream processor must continue as new events arrive.

questions.question: When was MapReduce published, what was it called?

options.text: Published in 2004, and called the algorithm behind Google's scalability
Published in 1998, called 'the Google File System', implemented in HDFS
Published in 2008, called 'the Hadoop algorithm', implemented in Spark and Flink
Published in 2004, called 'bulk synchronous parallel', implemented in Pregel

questions.explanation: Google published MapReduce in 2004 and it became closely associated with Google's scale. Independent implementations—including Hadoop, CouchDB, and MongoDB—then carried the model beyond Google's internal system.

questions.question: What was MapReduce's actual novelty?

options.text: Not novel as a programming model, but robustly scalable at Google
It was novel as a programming model and remains the state of the art
It was novel in neither respect and is no longer worth studying
It was novel in its query language, which is still widely used

questions.explanation: MapReduce's map/reduce programming idea was older and lower-level than existing parallel databases. Its breakthrough was making that model run reliably on commodity clusters at enormous scale. It remains useful pedagogically because its mechanics expose the core trade-offs of batch execution.

questions.question: What are the historical antecedents of batch processing?

options.text: Punch card tabulating machines, as in the 1890 US Census
The ENIAC of 1945 and the IBM System/360 of 1964
Punched tape systems from the 1920s, and nothing earlier
Batch processing has no genuine pre-computer ancestor

questions.explanation: Batch processing predates digital computers: Hollerith punch-card machines aggregated the 1890 census, and later IBM electromechanical sorters processed business records. MapReduce reused the same broad pattern of sorting bounded records into groups before aggregation.

questions.question: An nginx access log line reads: 216.58.210.78 - - [27/Feb/2015:17:55:11 +0000] 'GET /css/typography.css HTTP/1.1' 200 3377 'http://martin.kleppmann.com/' 'Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/40.0.2214.115'. What does it tell us? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That the request was made on February 27, 2015, at 17:55:11 UTC, for the file /css/typography.css, from the client IP address 216.58.210.78
That the user was not authenticated, so the remote_user field is set to a hyphen
That the response status was 200, meaning the request was successful, and the response was 3,377 bytes in size
That the browser was Chrome 40, and that the request carried no referrer header at all

questions.explanation: The log line does carry a referrer: the file was loaded because it was referenced in the page at that URL. There's a lot of information in one line — to interpret it you need to look at the definition of the log format. The example posits a web server that appends a line to a log file every time it serves a request, which makes the log append-only, immutable and bounded.

optionExplanations.a: The client address, UTC timestamp, request method, and path are explicit fields in the access-log format. They identify when, where, and from whom this request arrived.
optionExplanations.b: A hyphen in the configured remote-user field represents an unavailable authenticated username. It does not mean the client IP or all identity information is absent.
optionExplanations.c: HTTP status 200 records success, and the byte-count field records a 3,377-byte response body. Those positions must be interpreted using the server's declared log format.
optionExplanations.d: The user-agent does identify Chrome 40, but the quoted page URL is a referrer. Because the option denies that visible header, the combined claim is false.

questions.question: In the Unix pipeline for finding the five most popular pages, what does 'awk {print $7}' do?

options.text: It splits each line on whitespace and prints the seventh field
It prints the seventh line of the whole input file
It prints the seventh character of every input line
It counts seven fields per line and discards the rest

questions.explanation: The awk stage tokenizes each log line and emits field seven, which contains the requested URL in this log format. The preceding cat is optional; the explicit pipe simply makes the dataflow visible.

questions.question: The first sort produces no counts and no ranking. Why is it there?

options.text: Because sorting groups repeated URLs into adjacent lines
Because the head command requires its input to be sorted
Because awk emits its output fields in a random order
It is unnecessary and could be removed from the pipeline

questions.explanation: Adjacency is what makes counting possible without a hash table. This sort step is implicit in MapReduce.

questions.question: What do 'uniq -c' and 'sort -r -n' each do?

options.text: It collapses adjacent duplicate lines and -c prints the count
uniq removes duplicates without counting; sort -r -n sorts alphabetically in reverse
uniq counts all lines; sort -r -n sorts by URL numerically
uniq sorts and counts; sort -r -n reverses the file

questions.explanation: The uniq command filters out repeated lines in its input by checking whether two adjacent lines are the same. The -c option tells it to also output a counter: for every distinct URL, it reports how many times that URL appeared in the input. The word adjacent is the whole point — uniq has no memory of lines it saw earlier, which is why the preceding sort is mandatory.

questions.question: The output shows 4189 /favicon.ico, 3631 for an SSH keys article, 2124 for a schema evolution article, 1369 for /, and 915 for /css/typography.css. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The top five URLs account for 12,228 requests in total
The single most-requested URL accounts for about 34% of that total
The top entry, /favicon.ico, is arguably not a 'page' at all — it is the browser's tab icon
The top five URLs between them account for about 8,000 requests

questions.explanation: The five counts sum to 12,228, and 4,189 divided by 12,228 is about 34.3%. The favicon entry is a browser-requested icon asset rather than a content page, so all three statements are true.

optionExplanations.a: Adding the five displayed request counts gives 12,228. This checks the aggregate directly rather than estimating from the visual ranking.
optionExplanations.b: Dividing the largest count, 4,189, by 12,228 yields about 0.343, or 34 percent. The percentage refers to the shown top-five total, not all server traffic.
optionExplanations.c: A favicon is an icon fetched by the browser for tabs or bookmarks, not normally a content page a person intentionally visits. URL counts can therefore need semantic interpretation.
optionExplanations.d: The displayed values already exceed 8,000 after only the first three rows, and their exact sum is 12,228. The smaller total results from ignoring part of the data.

questions.question: You are asked to omit CSS files from the report, and separately to rank client IP addresses rather than pages. What changes?

options.text: Only the awk stage changes
The entire pipeline must be rewritten for each variation
The sort stage changes in the first case and head in the second
Those variations require a different toolchain, since awk cannot express either filter

questions.explanation: The pipeline's later stages still count and rank whatever key awk emits. Filtering CSS paths or switching from URL field 7 to client-IP field 1 therefore changes only awk, illustrating how a uniform streaming interface localizes a transformation.

questions.question: Which Unix tools are worth learning?

options.text: awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq and xargs
find, xargs and tar, citing the POSIX standard
python, perl and ruby, citing benchmark studies
hadoop, hive and pig, citing Google's paper

questions.explanation: Tools such as awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq, and xargs each handle a narrow operation and communicate through byte streams. Because their interfaces compose, a few commands can express surprisingly fast and flexible data analyses.

questions.question: A shell pipeline counts the most popular URLs in a web server log using awk '{print $7}'. An equivalent Ruby program instead reads line.split[6]. What does the Ruby version maintain, and why does the index differ?

options.text: A hash table of counters keyed by the URL; Ruby arrays are zero-indexed while awk fields start at one
A sorted array of every URL it has seen; the indices differ because the two tools read different log formats
A database connection opened per line; the indices genuinely point at two different fields of the log
No state at all between lines; the index is arbitrary and either value would have worked equally well

questions.explanation: The Ruby program keeps a hash table from URL to count, incrementing it for every log line before sorting the totals. awk numbers fields from 1, whereas Ruby arrays are zero-indexed, so awk's field 7 is line.split[6] in Ruby.

questions.question: How does a Unix pipeline execute differently from an equivalent in-process script?

options.text: Pipeline stages run concurrently and stream through bounded pipes
Only the syntax differs; the execution flow is identical
The Ruby version is always faster on the same input
The pipeline version is always the more readable of the two

questions.explanation: A shell pipeline runs its stages as concurrent processes and passes records incrementally through small buffers. The Ruby version builds the complete in-memory count table and only then sorts it, so their memory and streaming behavior diverge as the input grows.

questions.question: What do the Ruby script and the Unix pipeline each keep in memory?

options.text: The Ruby script keeps a hash table in memory; Unix sorts instead
Both keep hash tables, and the difference is the hash function used
Both sort their input, and the difference is the sorting algorithm
Each of the two avoids keeping any state in memory while it runs

questions.explanation: The hash-table approach uses memory proportional to the number of distinct URLs and can be fast when that set fits comfortably in RAM. Sorting can spill to disk and handle a much larger distinct set, at the cost of an external sort; total input lines alone do not decide the winner.

questions.question: Define working set, and what memory budget suffices for most small to mid-sized websites?

options.text: The amount of memory the job needs random access to
The working set is the total input size; 1 TB is needed
The working set is the number of log lines; 1 GB per million lines is needed
The working set is the output size; no memory is needed

questions.explanation: The working set is the data that requires random access, not the total input size. Counting a million identical URLs still needs one table entry; memory grows with the number of distinct URLs, and roughly 1 GB is often enough for a small or medium website.

questions.question: When the working set exceeds available memory, why does sorting win?

options.text: Because sorting spills sorted chunks to disk and merges them
Because sorting uses less CPU than hashing
Because sorting requires no disk at all
Because hash tables cannot be spilled to disk in any implementation

questions.explanation: The GNU Coreutils sort utility on Linux automatically handles larger-than-memory datasets by spilling to disk, and automatically parallelizes sorting across multiple CPU cores — so it easily scales to large datasets without running out of memory, and the bottleneck becomes the rate at which the input file can be read from disk.

questions.question: Who invented Unix pipes, when, and with what analogy?

options.text: Doug McIlroy, in 1964
Ken Thompson in 1970, with a plumbing analogy
Dennis Ritchie in 1978, with an assembly-line analogy
Eric Raymond in 1999, with a Lego analogy

questions.explanation: 1964 for the description, with the garden-hose image that gave pipes their name.

questions.question: Which statements accurately represent the Unix philosophy published in 1978? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh rather than complicate old programs by adding new 'features'

Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program. Don't clutter output with extraneous information, avoid stringently columnar or binary input formats, and don't insist on interactive input
Design and build software, even operating systems, to be tried early, ideally within weeks. Don't hesitate to throw away the clumsy parts and rebuild them
Use unskilled help in preference to building tools, since the detour to build a tool is always wasteful in the end

questions.explanation: Small programs with stable stream interfaces can be recombined into unanticipated workflows. Early feedback and willingness to replace clumsy pieces make the philosophy compatible with iterative delivery.

optionExplanations.a: Keeping each program focused makes it composable and replaceable; new behavior is built by combining tools rather than accumulating unrelated features in one program.
optionExplanations.b: Stable, uncluttered stream output allows an unknown future program to consume today's result. Interactive-only or rigid private formats would prevent that composition.
optionExplanations.c: Trying software early exposes awkward design while replacement is still affordable. The philosophy favors experimentation and rebuilding clumsy pieces over defending an initial design.
optionExplanations.d: The published principle says to build tools instead of relying on unskilled help when a tool will pay off. Reversing that advice removes the automation and reuse the philosophy promotes.

questions.question: Which properties characterize the Unix philosophy in practice?

options.text: Automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration and experimentation
Reliability, scalability, maintainability, security and compliance — compared to enterprise database design
Speed, cost, simplicity, safety and portability — compared to the cloud
The five properties are unnamed

questions.explanation: Small tools and scripts make a workflow easy to automate, inspect, change, and rerun. That short feedback loop encourages experiments and decomposes large work into reversible stages—the same organizational advantages later emphasized by Agile and DevOps.

questions.question: Why is sort the exemplar Unix tool here?

options.text: Because it handles datasets larger than memory by spilling to disk
Because it is the fastest tool, and there is no sting
Because it is the simplest tool, and the sting is that it is slow
Because it does many things, and the sting is that it violates the philosophy

questions.explanation: sort is strong because it spills runs to disk, merges them, and can use multiple CPU cores rather than assuming everything fits in memory. Yet sorting alone produces little value; the useful analysis emerges when it is connected to stages such as awk and uniq.

questions.question: What is the uniform interface in Unix, precisely?

options.text: A file, or more precisely a file descriptor
A record, defined as a tuple of typed fields
A stream of structured objects
A pipe, which is distinct from a file

questions.explanation: In Unix, that interface is a file (or, more precisely, a file descriptor). A file is just an ordered sequence of bytes. Because the interface is so simple, many different things can be represented with it: - an actual file on the filesystem - a communication channel to another process (Unix socket, stdin, stdout) - a device driver (say /dev/audio or /dev/lp0) - a socket representing a TCP connection The logic: If you want to be able to connect any program's output to any program's input, that means that all programs must use the same input/output interface.

questions.question: Which record separator do awk, sort, uniq and head all agree on?

options.text: A list of records separated by the newline character
They agree on the tab character; the comma would have been better
They agree on 0x1E already, which is ideal
Each tool picks its own record separator, so the choice is arbitrary

questions.explanation: All stages must agree on record boundaries to compose reliably. Unix convention chose newline (0x0A), even though the dedicated ASCII record-separator byte 0x1E would have expressed that role more explicitly.

questions.question: What is unsatisfying about ASCII text as a uniform interface?

options.text: That {print $7} is not very readable
It is too slow to parse
It cannot represent binary data at all
Nothing is unsatisfying: positional field references are perfectly readable

questions.explanation: Positional field references are the cost of an untyped interface.

questions.question: How rare is Unix-grade composability today?

options.text: That it is now the exception rather than the norm
It is the norm; most modern tools compose as well as Unix tools
It is universal within cloud platforms
It has improved steadily since 1978

questions.explanation: When every tool invents a private format, useful data becomes trapped behind conversion code. Shared textual or schema-based interfaces keep independently written stages composable.

questions.question: What are stdin and stdout bound to by default?

options.text: stdin from the keyboard and stdout to the screen
Each is bound to a file by default, and only a pipe can change that
Each is bound to the network by default, with files as the exception
They cannot be rebound

questions.explanation: Without redirection, a process reads stdin from the keyboard and writes stdout to the terminal. File redirection and pipes replace those endpoints, allowing the same program to participate in many workflows without knowing who produces or consumes its bytes.

questions.question: What are the existing names for a program not knowing where its input comes from?

options.text: Loose coupling, late binding, or inversion of control
Encapsulation, abstraction and polymorphism
Dependency injection, service location and reflection
Modularity, cohesion and coupling

questions.explanation: Loose coupling means a component depends on an interface rather than the identity of its producer or consumer. Late binding and inversion of control describe the same separation from different traditions.

questions.question: You want to add stages that translate user-agent strings into browser identifiers and IP addresses into country codes. What must your programs do?

options.text: Read from stdin and write to stdout
Your program must register with sort and declare its schema
Your program must be written in C and linked against sort
Your program must implement a plugin interface

questions.explanation: A custom stage only needs to read stdin and write stdout in the agreed record format. sort sees the same byte stream whether its neighbor is a built-in tool or custom code, which separates each stage's logic from pipeline wiring.

questions.question: What are the limits of stdin/stdout wiring? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Programs that need multiple inputs or outputs are possible but tricky
You can't pipe a program's output into a network connection

If a program directly opens files for reading and writing, or starts another program as a subprocess, or opens a network connection, then that I/O is wired up by the program itself — it can still be configurable via command-line options, but the flexibility of wiring up inputs and outputs in a shell is reduced
Unix programs are unable to read from files at all, only from standard input

questions.explanation: stdin and stdout provide one input and one output stream. Multiple streams, direct file access, subprocesses, or sockets require extra APIs or configuration and therefore reduce shell-level rewiring.

optionExplanations.a: A process naturally has only one standard input and one standard output stream, so several independent inputs or outputs require conventions such as files, descriptors, or helper processes.
optionExplanations.b: A shell pipe connects local process streams, not directly a remote socket. A program such as netcat can bridge the stream, but that helper owns the network connection.
optionExplanations.c: When code opens its own files, subprocesses, or sockets, those endpoints are hidden behind program-specific configuration. The shell can no longer freely rewire the whole dataflow.
optionExplanations.d: Unix programs can read ordinary files directly and can also receive a file through standard input. The limitation concerns composable wiring, not an inability to access files.

questions.question: Why do Unix tools make it easy to see what is going on? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Inputs stay immutable, so commands can be rerun safely
Any pipeline stage can be inspected through a pager such as less
Intermediate output can be saved so later stages restart independently
A built-in optimizer explains the globally chosen execution plan

questions.explanation: So even though Unix tools are quite blunt, simple tools compared to a query optimizer of a relational database, they remain amazingly useful, especially for experimentation.

optionExplanations.a: Immutable input lets an operator rerun a command without destroying the source, making experiments and debugging reproducible. Mutation would erase the evidence needed to inspect a failure.
optionExplanations.b: Because each stage emits a normal byte stream, a pager can be inserted to inspect exactly what that stage produced. This makes the pipeline observable one boundary at a time.
optionExplanations.c: Saving an intermediate stream creates a restart point and lets later stages be tested independently. It trades storage for easier diagnosis and incremental experimentation.
optionExplanations.d: Classic Unix pipelines have no global cost-based optimizer explaining a chosen plan. Their transparency comes from simple explicit stages, not automated whole-pipeline planning.

questions.question: What is the biggest limitation of Unix tools?

options.text: That they run only on a single machine
That they only handle text, not binary data
That they cannot be scripted
That they have no fault tolerance

questions.explanation: Unix pipelines scale across cores on one host but do not distribute storage and tasks across a cluster. Hadoop extends the compositional idea with HDFS, scheduling, shuffle, and retry.

questions.question: Complete and defend the analogy: MapReduce is a bit like Unix tools, but…?

options.text: Distributed across potentially thousands of machines
…with a declarative query language instead of shell commands
…running on a single very large machine
…operating on streams rather than files

questions.explanation: The analogy is about composition and framework-owned plumbing, not identical execution. A mapper or reducer has a narrow record-processing interface while Hadoop supplies distributed storage, scheduling, shuffle, and retry across many machines.

questions.question: What two Unix-like restraints does a MapReduce job observe?

options.text: It does not modify its input and has no side effects
It modifies the input in place and appends to existing outputs
It may have arbitrary side effects but must not modify the input
It may modify the input but must have no side effects

questions.explanation: A MapReduce job treats its input as immutable and confines its visible effect to new output files written sequentially. That discipline lets the framework retry a failed task without corrupting the source or duplicating external actions.

questions.question: What do MapReduce jobs use instead of stdin and stdout, and what is Hadoop's implementation?

options.text: HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System
They use TCP sockets; the implementation is YARN
They use local disks; the implementation is ext4
They use a message queue; the implementation is Kafka

questions.explanation: Files and pipes are substituted by a distributed filesystem — the key structural claim.

questions.question: Which storage systems are alternatives to a distributed filesystem? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Other distributed filesystems besides HDFS, such as GlusterFS and the Quantcast File System (QFS)
Object storage services such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage and OpenStack Swift, which are similar in many ways
Any of these can serve as the storage layer for a batch job, since the same distributed-filesystem principles apply
Relational databases such as PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle, which reach petabyte scale by adding read replicas

questions.explanation: HDFS, other distributed filesystems, and object stores all provide durable distributed input. HDFS can additionally schedule computation beside a local replica, while object stores usually separate storage and compute.

optionExplanations.a: GlusterFS and QFS also distribute durable file blocks across machines, so a batch engine can read partitioned input from them much as it does from HDFS.
optionExplanations.b: Object stores provide durable, scalable objects accessible by many workers and can serve as batch input and output. They usually separate compute placement from storage placement.
optionExplanations.c: The essential requirement is durable distributed data that workers can partition and process. Scheduling and locality details differ, but the batch model is not tied exclusively to HDFS.
optionExplanations.d: Relational databases are useful sources for some jobs, but ordinary read replicas do not make them equivalent to petabyte-scale distributed filesystems or object stores for scan-heavy batch storage.

questions.question: Which principle is HDFS based on?

options.text: The shared-nothing principle
The shared-disk principle, in contrast to shared-nothing
The shared-memory principle, in contrast to message passing
The shared-everything principle, in contrast to partitioning

questions.explanation: HDFS spreads storage across ordinary machines whose disks are independent: the shared-nothing model. NAS and SAN designs instead put data behind a centralized shared-disk appliance, often using specialized hardware or networking.

questions.question: How is HDFS put together?

options.text: A daemon on each machine exposing a network file service
It consists of a single storage server with attached disks
It consists of daemons only, with no central metadata server
It consists of a NameNode only, with data stored in S3

questions.explanation: Each storage node runs a daemon that serves its local blocks, while central metadata maps files to those blocks. Replication lets another node supply a block after disk or machine failure.

questions.question: How does HDFS survive machine and disk failure?

options.text: Replicated across several machines, or erasure-coded
It relies on RAID within each individual machine only
It relies on nightly backups written out to tape
It does not tolerate disk failure at all by design

questions.explanation: HDFS stores redundant information across machines so one disk or host can fail without losing a block. It may keep full replicas or use erasure coding for lower storage overhead; unlike RAID, recovery happens over an ordinary datacenter network.

questions.question: State MapReduce's four-step pattern and its log-analysis counterparts. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Read a set of input files and break it up into records — in the web server log example, each record is one line in the log, so the newline is the record separator
Call the mapper function to extract a key and value from each input record — here the mapper function is awk {print $7}: it extracts the URL as the key and leaves the value empty
Sort all of the key-value pairs by key — in the log example this is done by the first sort command
Call the reducer to iterate over the sorted key-value pairs — in the log example this is implemented by the second sort command in the pipeline

questions.explanation: The reducer in the log example is uniq -c, which collapses adjacent duplicates and counts them; the second sort is a separate ordering step. Four steps, mapping exactly onto the four pipeline stages.

optionExplanations.a: The input reader splits files into records before user mapping code runs. In a line-oriented web log, the newline boundary naturally defines one request record.
optionExplanations.b: The mapper transforms each record into zero or more key-value pairs; extracting the URL makes requests for the same URL share a grouping key.
optionExplanations.c: Sorting by key brings equal URLs together so the reducer can process each key's complete group. This is framework-managed data movement rather than application code.
optionExplanations.d: The reducer counterpart is the counting operation, such as uniq -c, while the second sort ranks the resulting counts. Confusing the ranking sort with reduction misidentifies the stages.

questions.question: Of the four steps, which do you write?

options.text: Steps 2 and 4 — the map and reduce functions
You write all four steps
You write only step 3; the framework supplies the rest
The framework supplies all four steps

questions.explanation: User code supplies map and reduce; the framework always performs the intervening partition and sort. Later dataflow engines make that data movement conditional on what each graph edge actually needs.

questions.question: How is a mapper invoked on its input?

options.text: Once per input record, emitting zero or more key-value pairs
It is called once per file and maintains state across records
It must generate exactly one key-value pair per record
It is called once per key and receives all matching records

questions.explanation: The mapper handles each input record independently and may emit any number of key-value pairs, including none. Keeping no hidden state between records allows the framework to split, reorder, and retry map tasks safely.

questions.question: State the reducer's contract?

options.text: It collects all values for one key and calls the reducer on them
It receives one key-value pair at a time with no grouping
It receives a fully materialized list of all values for a key
It receives the entire dataset and must group it itself

questions.explanation: An iterator rather than a list is what lets a key's value set exceed memory.

questions.question: The log pipeline had a second sort. How do you get that in MapReduce?

options.text: By chaining a second job onto the first job's output
By calling sort from inside the reducer function itself
By configuring the framework to perform the sort twice
A second sort is not possible within MapReduce at all

questions.explanation: One sort per job, so a second sort means a second job.

questions.question: What does MapReduce add over a Unix pipeline?

options.text: That it parallelizes across machines without explicit parallel code
It adds a declarative query language over the input files
It adds transactions spanning several machines
It adds low-latency responses to interactive queries

questions.explanation: This is the Unix separation of logic and wiring, applied across a cluster.

questions.question: What are mappers and reducers actually written in?

options.text: Usually as functions in a conventional programming language
Only standard Unix tools may be used as mappers
Only SQL may be used to express the computation
Only C++ may be used, as is the case at Google

questions.explanation: Mappers and reducers are ordinary functions in a general-purpose language. The framework supplies their distributed invocation, data transfer, retries, and output publication.

questions.question: What determines the map-side parallelism?

options.text: A directory in HDFS, with each file block as a partition
You choose the number of mappers, and the scheduler places them randomly
The number of mappers equals the number of machines, and data is copied to them
One mapper per input record, placed by hash

questions.explanation: Each input file block becomes a map partition. When resources allow, the scheduler places the mapper on a machine that already stores a replica, copying the much smaller program there and avoiding a network transfer of the large input.

questions.question: Contrast how the numbers of map and reduce tasks are determined?

options.text: Map tasks by the input blocks; reduce tasks by configuration
Both counts are set explicitly in the job configuration
Both counts are determined by the number of input blocks
Keys reach reducers by range partitioning rather than hashing

questions.explanation: Input block layout determines mapper count, configuration determines reducer count, and hashing sends every occurrence of one key to the same reducer.

questions.question: Why does the sort happen in stages?

options.text: Because the dataset is too large to sort on one machine
Mapper output goes straight to HDFS, sorted globally in one pass
Mapper output is kept entirely in memory
Mapper output is sorted by the reducers, not the mappers

questions.explanation: Per-mapper sorted partitions on local disk, merged later by reducers.

questions.question: What does the MapReduce shuffle do, and why is its name misleading?

options.text: Partition, sort, and copy mapper output so equal keys reach the same reducer
The shuffle is the random reassignment of keys to reducers; the name is apt
The shuffle is the sorting step only; the name is apt
The shuffle is the reduce phase itself, and nothing about the name is misleading

questions.explanation: The shuffle deterministically partitions mapper records by key, sorts each reducer's partition, and transfers those partitions across the network. The name is misleading because no random permutation occurs.

questions.question: How does a reducer receive mapper output in key order?

options.text: It merge-sorts the partition files fetched from every mapper
The reducer sorts the fetched files itself before processing
The reducer writes output to its local disk only, with no replication
The reducer receives unsorted records and must group them in memory

questions.explanation: Each reducer fetches its partition from every mapper and merge-sorts those files so equal keys are adjacent. The reducer streams the values for one key through an iterator, emits zero or more records, and publishes its output to replicated distributed storage.

questions.question: Why must a complex batch workflow chain multiple MapReduce jobs?

options.text: One job provides only one map-shuffle-reduce stage
Jobs are chained by an explicit workflow API in Hadoop MapReduce
Jobs are chained through in-memory pipes
Jobs cannot be chained

questions.explanation: Directory names are the entire chaining mechanism — chained jobs are less like pipelines of Unix commands, which pass output as input directly using only a small in-memory buffer, and more like a sequence of commands where each command's output is written to a temporary file and the next command reads from that file.

questions.question: When is a batch job's output valid?

options.text: Only when the job completes successfully
Partial output is valid; jobs may start as soon as any input appears
The MapReduce framework enforces dependencies internally
HDFS enforces dependencies through file locks

questions.explanation: All-or-nothing output, with an external scheduler enforcing ordering.

questions.question: How big do workflows get?

options.text: Fifty to a hundred MapReduce jobs
Workflows rarely exceed 5 jobs; no tooling is needed
Workflows reach thousands of jobs; only Oozie can manage them
Workflows are always single jobs in practice

questions.explanation: Large recommendation pipelines may chain 50–100 jobs, so manually coordinating directory dependencies becomes fragile. Workflow schedulers such as Oozie, Azkaban, Luigi, Airflow, and Pinball launch jobs only after their inputs are successfully available.

questions.question: When is a join necessary?

options.text: A foreign key, a document reference, or a graph edge
A join is necessary only in relational models; denormalization removes it entirely
A join is never necessary in batch processing
Joins matter only for graph-shaped data, so denormalization is beside the point

questions.explanation: A join follows an association—foreign key, document reference, or graph edge—to combine records from both sides. Denormalization copies the referenced attributes into the first record, trading update duplication and consistency work for avoiding the read-time join.

questions.question: What does MapReduce do instead of using indexes?

options.text: It reads the entire contents of all its input files
MapReduce builds indexes on the fly for each join
MapReduce uses HDFS indexes, which are always faster than scans
MapReduce refuses joins entirely

questions.explanation: In a batch context, join means resolving all occurrences of some association within a dataset — the data for all users simultaneously, not merely looking up the data for one particular user, which would be done far more efficiently with an index.

questions.question: What is the activity side of a user-profile join commonly called?

options.text: Clickstream data
Two fact tables joined on a timestamp
Two dimension tables joined on a surrogate key
A single denormalized table requiring no join

questions.explanation: Clickstream events are the fact table: many time-stamped actions keyed by user ID. User profiles are a dimension table: relatively stable descriptive attributes. Joining them lets an analysis group behavior by age or other profile properties without repeating those properties in every event.

questions.question: Why would querying the user database for every event perform poorly? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The processing throughput would be limited by the round-trip time to the database server
The effectiveness of a local cache would depend very much on the distribution of data
Running a large number of queries in parallel could easily overwhelm the database
The database would refuse to accept that many concurrent connections

questions.explanation: It is possible, but it would most likely suffer from very poor performance. Two rules follow: in order to achieve good throughput in a batch process, the computation must be local to one machine as much as possible — making random-access requests over the network for every record you want to process is too slow. And querying a remote database would mean the batch job becomes nondeterministic, because the data in the remote database might change.

optionExplanations.a: A synchronous remote lookup adds at least one network round trip per event, putting database latency directly on the critical path and severely limiting batch throughput.
optionExplanations.b: A cache helps only when accesses have enough locality and the working set fits. Uniformly distributed user IDs can produce a low hit rate and preserve most remote lookups.
optionExplanations.c: Thousands of batch tasks can issue queries concurrently and overload connection pools, CPU, or I/O on the operational database. The batch job then harms both itself and production traffic.
optionExplanations.d: Databases do not universally reject parallel clients; most are designed for concurrency. The problem is finite capacity and expensive per-record network access, not a categorical connection rule.

questions.question: For a join between a large activity dataset and user profiles, what is preferable to making a random database lookup for every activity event, and where should the copied profile data live?

options.text: Put a copy of the user database in the distributed filesystem
Query the live database from the reducer rather than the mapper
Replicate the activity log into the database
Cache the user database in each mapper's memory from the network

questions.explanation: Copying the profile data into the distributed filesystem turns the join into sequential cluster I/O. It avoids a fragile random database request for every activity event.

questions.question: What does each mapper emit in a reduce-side join of activity events and user profiles?

options.text: User ID to event, and user ID to profile
Both sets emit the event timestamp as the key
Only the activity mappers emit; the user database is loaded into memory
Both sets emit the date of birth as the key

questions.explanation: Both mapper sets use user ID as the key but emit differently tagged values: an activity event or a profile record. The shuffle groups one user's records at one reducer, making the join local rather than a remote lookup per event.

questions.question: In a reduce-side sort-merge join, which technique ensures that the reducer receives the user-profile record before that user's activity events?

options.text: Secondary sort, so the database record arrives first
Primary sort, which orders by key only
Total order partitioning, which orders reducers
Combiner ordering, which pre-aggregates on the map side

questions.explanation: Secondary sort uses the composite ordering of reducer input: partition by user ID, then order within that user by record type and timestamp. The profile arrives first, allowing the reducer to cache it once before streaming the activity events.

questions.question: How often does a reducer need to load each user's profile during a secondary-sorted join?

options.text: Once per user ID, before streaming that user's activity events
The reducer is called once per activity event and queries the user database
The reducer buffers all records for all users in memory
The reducer emits the raw records unchanged

questions.explanation: The reducer function is called once for every user ID, and thanks to the secondary sort, the first value is expected to be the date-of-birth record from the user database. The reducer stores the date of birth in a local variable and then iterates over the activity events with the same user ID, outputting pairs of viewed-url and viewer-age-in-years. Downstream: Subsequent MapReduce jobs could then calculate the distribution of viewer ages for each URL, and cluster by age group.

questions.question: Explain the 'mappers send messages to the reducers' metaphor?

options.text: The mappers as senders and the reducers as recipients
The key is literally an IP address and port
The mappers open TCP connections to the reducers directly
The metaphor applies only to Pregel, not to MapReduce

questions.explanation: The key acts like a logical destination: every mapper emits records addressed by key, and partitioning routes equal keys to the same reducer. The application never manages network addresses.

questions.question: What two aspects does MapReduce separate?

options.text: It separates the network communication from the application logic
It separates reads from writes, which buys durability
It separates storage from compute, which buys elasticity
It separates mappers from reducers, which buys nothing extra

questions.explanation: Communication separated from logic, with transparent retries as a bonus.

questions.question: What is the second common use of the 'bring related data together' pattern?

options.text: Grouping records by some key, as SQL's GROUP BY does
Filtering records, implemented in the reducer
Sorting records, implemented by the framework alone
Deduplicating records, implemented by a combiner

questions.explanation: The same shuffle used for joins can implement SQL-style GROUP BY. Mappers emit the grouping key, partitioning sends equal keys to one reducer, and sorting makes the group's records adjacent for counting, summing, or top-k aggregation.

questions.question: What is sessionization?

options.text: Collating all activity events for one user session
Splitting one user's events across many servers for load balancing
Counting total page views per day
Deduplicating events by timestamp

questions.explanation: Sessionization groups events by a session cookie or user ID and orders them to reconstruct one visit. The result supports analyses such as navigation paths, funnels, and sequences of actions even when the original events came from many web servers.

questions.question: What breaks the 'bring all records with the same key to the same place' pattern?

options.text: A very large amount of data for a single key
Too many distinct keys, known as fan-out
Too few reducers, known as underpartitioning
Unsorted input, known as disorder

questions.explanation: A hot key breaks balanced partitioning because all of its records normally go to one reducer. Such skew—also called a hot spot, hot key, or linchpin object—can leave one machine overloaded while the rest finish early.

questions.question: Describe the skewed join method in Pig?

options.text: It samples first to find hot keys, then spreads them over reducers
It routes all of the hot-key records to a single dedicated reducer
It drops the hot-key records and processes them in a later pass
It hashes the hot keys twice in order to spread them further

questions.explanation: Pig first samples the input to discover hot keys. It then distributes one hot key's large side randomly across several reducers and replicates the matching records from the other side, trading controlled duplication for parallelism.

questions.question: How does Pig distribute a join key that is too hot for one reducer?

options.text: Sample hot keys and shard them across reducers
All three use sampling jobs and random reducer assignment
All three require explicit hot-key specification
Pig requires explicit keys; Crunch and Hive use sampling

questions.explanation: Pig discovers hot keys by sampling and shards them across reducers. Crunch requires the keys to be declared explicitly. Hive records them in table metadata, stores their records separately, and uses a map-side join for those keys.

questions.question: For grouping and aggregating by a hot key, which two-stage technique works?

options.text: A first stage groups a random subset, and a second combines them
A single stage configured with a larger number of reducers
A first stage that drops hot keys and a second that reprocesses them
Two stages which each aggregate the full dataset independently

questions.explanation: Partial aggregation shrinks the data before the final combine.

questions.question: Why are sort-merge joins called reduce-side joins?

options.text: Because the join logic runs in the reducers
Because the join happens in the mappers; the advantage is speed
Because the reducers sort; the advantage is that no assumptions are needed and there is no cost
Because HDFS performs the join; the disadvantage is network load

questions.explanation: A reduce-side join accepts arbitrary input layouts because the shuffle repartitions both sides by join key. That generality costs network transfer, sorting, and reducer work.

questions.question: Which join avoids reducers and sorting when its inputs are suitably prepared?

options.text: A map-side join
It requires more reducers and extra sorting
It requires the input to be unsorted and unpartitioned
It requires a second job to merge results

questions.explanation: A map-side join is possible only when the inputs already satisfy useful size or partitioning assumptions. Each mapper reads its input block and the matching data directly, so the job needs no reducer, shuffle, or global sort.

questions.question: What size condition enables a broadcast hash join?

options.text: A large dataset joined with one small enough to fit in memory
Both inputs must be small; the name refers to broadcasting to reducers
The small input is partitioned; the name refers to a hash partitioner
The large input is loaded into memory; the name is arbitrary

questions.explanation: A broadcast hash join requires one input small enough to fit in every mapper's memory. Each mapper builds a hash table from that complete input and probes it while scanning one large-input partition: the data is broadcast, and lookup is by hash.

questions.question: What is the alternative to an in-memory hash table for the small join input?

options.text: Keep the small input in a read-only index on local disk
Store it in a remote database and query that once per record
Store it in HDFS and read it back once per input record
Loading it fully into memory is the only workable option here

questions.explanation: The page cache does the caching for you, lifting the memory constraint.

questions.question: What precondition lets matching hash buckets be joined locally?

options.text: If both inputs are partitioned the same way
All mappers load the whole user database, as in a broadcast join
Each mapper reads all partitions of both datasets
The partitions must differ between the two sides

questions.explanation: Matching hash buckets guarantee that records capable of joining are in the same-numbered partitions. Each mapper reads one bucket from each input, so with ten balanced buckets it builds a hash table for roughly one tenth of the data instead of the whole input.

questions.question: What partition-count condition must a partitioned hash join satisfy?

options.text: Both inputs must have the same number of partitions
It works if either input is partitioned; Hive calls it a MapJoin
It works if both are sorted but not partitioned; Hive calls it a merge join
It works unconditionally; Hive calls it a skewed join

questions.explanation: A partitioned hash join requires both inputs to use the same partition count, join key, and hash function. Hive calls this a bucketed map join; prior jobs or table metadata must establish the compatible layout.

questions.question: What extra precondition does a map-side merge join need?

options.text: Both inputs must be partitioned and sorted on the same key
The inputs must be small enough to fit in memory
The inputs must be unsorted, since the mapper sorts them
The inputs must be in the same file

questions.explanation: A map-side merge join additionally requires both inputs to be sorted by the join key. A mapper can then advance through both files incrementally without a hash table. Keeping it separate can still make sense when the prepared datasets serve other consumers.

questions.question: How does choosing a broadcast hash join versus a partitioned hash join affect output partitioning?

options.text: Reduce-side output is sorted by join key; map-side inherits the large input's layout
Both joins produce output sorted by the join key; metadata lives in HDFS block headers
Output layout is unaffected by either kind of join, so the metadata is unnecessary
Map-side joins produce unsorted output; metadata lives in ZooKeeper

questions.explanation: A reduce-side join creates output partitioned and sorted by the join key. A map-side join inherits the large input's layout, whether broadcast or partitioned. HCatalog and the Hive metastore record the partition count, keys, and sort layout needed to choose safely.

questions.question: How do OLTP and analytical workloads differ in their data-access pattern?

options.text: OLTP looks up a few records by key; analytics scans in bulk
Batch processing is really a form of transaction processing
Batch processing is identical to analytics in every respect
Batch processing always produces human-readable reports

questions.explanation: OLTP retrieves or changes a small number of records by key, whereas analytics scans and aggregates many records. Batch jobs usually resemble the latter access pattern but may produce files or indexes instead of reports.

questions.question: What was MapReduce originally built for at Google?

options.text: Building the search index for Google's search engine
Building the web crawl itself, in 50 to 100 jobs
Computing PageRank scores, in one single job
Serving live search queries, in 5 to 10 jobs

questions.explanation: Note the contrast in scale: 5 to 10 jobs for search indexing versus 50 to 100 for recommendation systems.

questions.question: Why is batch processing well suited to building a document-partitioned search index?

options.text: Each mapper can build one immutable index partition independently
The mappers build the index and the reducers query it; outputs are mutable
A single reducer builds a global index; outputs are mutable
Indexes are built at query time, so there are no output files

questions.explanation: If you need to perform a full-text search over a fixed set of documents, then a batch process is a very effective way of building the indexes: the mappers partition the set of documents as needed, each reducer builds the index for its partition, and the index files are written to the distributed filesystem. The kind of index: Building such document-partitioned indexes parallelizes very well. Immutability: Since querying a search index by keyword is a read-only operation, these index files are immutable once they have been created.

questions.question: What is the simplest way to refresh a search index?

options.text: Rebuild and atomically replace the whole index
Full rebuild is cheap and incremental is expensive
Only incremental indexing is possible
Only full rebuilds are possible

questions.explanation: Simplicity versus efficiency, with segment merging as the incremental mechanism.

questions.question: Which machine learning outputs come out of batch jobs?

options.text: Classifiers and recommendation systems
Only classifiers; the output is always a report
Only recommendation systems; the output stays in HDFS
Neither: batch jobs can only build search indexes, not machine learning models

questions.explanation: Two families, both producing databases that must be served from outside Hadoop.

questions.question: Why is writing to the database from inside a mapper or reducer a bad idea? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One network request per record destroys batch throughput
Many parallel tasks can overwhelm the destination database
External writes expose partial and speculative task effects
Databases accept only one writer, so parallel clients are rejected

questions.explanation: Per-record remote calls are slow, parallel tasks may overload the database, and retries or speculative attempts can duplicate visible writes. Firewall access does not solve those correctness and throughput problems.

optionExplanations.a: A remote write for every record replaces sequential local processing with network latency and protocol overhead. This defeats the high-throughput access pattern batch systems depend on.
optionExplanations.b: Many mapper and reducer instances run in parallel, so their combined write load can saturate the destination's connections, indexes, locks, or storage bandwidth.
optionExplanations.c: Tasks may be retried or speculatively duplicated, exposing partial output and duplicate writes outside the framework's atomic file publication. External side effects are not automatically rolled back.
optionExplanations.d: Most databases accept multiple writers and coordinate them with transactions or concurrency control. The risk is overload and duplicated effects, not an inherent single-writer restriction.

questions.question: State MapReduce's all-or-nothing guarantee?

options.text: A clean all-or-nothing guarantee on job output
Partial output is visible during execution and cleaned up afterward
Every task's output is visible, including retries
The guarantee applies only to reducers, not mappers

questions.explanation: Exactly-once effect from at-least-once execution, achieved by discarding losers.

questions.question: What is the right way to ship batch output into a serving database?

options.text: Build a new database inside the job and write it out as files
Write directly to the production database from the reducer, in batches
Export to CSV and import manually
Stream the output through a message queue into the database

questions.explanation: When loading data into Voldemort, the server continues serving requests to the old data files while the new data files are copied from the distributed filesystem to the server's local disk; once copying is complete, the server atomically switches over to querying the new files. If anything goes wrong it can easily switch back to the old files again, since they are still there and immutable.

questions.question: State the discipline that MapReduce inherits from Unix about how a job treats its input and its output, and the maintainability benefits that follow. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Read immutable input and replace output without other side effects
Rebuild bad output with corrected code or restore a prior output
Reversible output lets teams iterate more quickly
Keep failed tasks' partial output so retries can reuse it

questions.explanation: Partial output of a failed task is discarded, precisely so that the retry is invisible — the framework reschedules the task and runs it again. Also on the list: the same set of files can be used as input for various different jobs, including monitoring jobs that calculate metrics and evaluate whether a job's output has the expected characteristics — for example by comparing it to the output from the previous run and measuring discrepancies.

optionExplanations.a: Reading immutable input and publishing replacement output keeps a task free of hidden side effects. A retry can recompute the same result without repairing partially mutated source data.
optionExplanations.b: Because outputs are derived, incorrect results can be deleted and rebuilt from unchanged inputs or replaced by a known-good version. Recovery does not require undoing arbitrary updates.
optionExplanations.c: Reversible derived output lowers the cost of trying new code, comparing versions, and rolling back. That operational freedom improves maintainability as well as fault recovery.
optionExplanations.d: Failed-task output is deliberately discarded because it may be incomplete or duplicated. Reusing it would make retries observe and preserve an uncertain partial result.

questions.question: What advantage do schema-aware formats such as Avro and Parquet have over ad hoc text?

options.text: They avoid repeated text parsing and support compatible schema evolution
Hadoop uses text files and Unix uses structured formats
The two are alike in this respect, since both of them pass around untyped text records
Hadoop eliminates the need for any interface

questions.explanation: Plain-text pipelines repeatedly interpret delimiters and fields at each stage. Avro and Parquet carry a schema and use efficient structured encodings, reducing parsing overhead while allowing compatible schema changes over time.

questions.question: Why was the MapReduce paper 'not at all new'?

options.text: Because those algorithms already existed in MPP databases
Because MapReduce was copied from Hadoop
Because MapReduce was described in the 1978 Unix paper
Because MPP databases postdate MapReduce

questions.explanation: Generality is the difference, not the algorithms.

questions.question: What does a database require of your data that a distributed filesystem does not?

options.text: Because a distributed filesystem accepts bytes in any format
Databases require sorted input; filesystems do not
Databases require immutable data; filesystems allow mutation
The requirements the two place on incoming data are identical

questions.explanation: Hadoop opened up the possibility of indiscriminately dumping data into HDFS and only later figuring out how to process it further, whereas MPP databases typically require careful up-front modeling of the data and query patterns before importing the data into the database's proprietary storage format. From a purist's point of view careful modeling and import is desirable because users have better-quality data to work with — but in practice, simply making data available quickly, even in a quirky, difficult-to-use, raw format, is often more valuable than trying to decide on the ideal data model up front.

questions.question: Which named ideas describe raw-first data collection? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data lake or enterprise data hub: bringing data from various parts of a large organization together in one place is valuable, because it enables joins across datasets that were previously disparate — and the careful schema design required by an MPP database slows down that centralized data collection, so collecting data in its raw form and worrying about schema design later speeds it up

Schema-on-read: indiscriminate data dumping shifts the burden of interpreting the data from the producer to the consumer, which can be an advantage if the producer and consumers are different teams with different priorities — and there may not even be one ideal data model, but rather different views onto the data that are suitable for different purposes
The sushi principle: 'raw data is better'
The waterfall principle: design the schema completely before any data is loaded, so that every consumer afterwards reads the data through one agreed model

questions.explanation: Schema-on-read stores raw bytes first and interprets them when a job runs. That flexibility supports many future uses, but validation errors surface later than with schema-on-write.

optionExplanations.a: A data lake or enterprise hub collects disparate raw datasets before forcing one warehouse schema, enabling later cross-source joins. It prioritizes acquisition speed and future reuse.
optionExplanations.b: Schema-on-read lets each consumer interpret stored bytes for its own purpose when it reads them. The flexibility shifts validation and modeling work from ingestion to consumption.
optionExplanations.c: The sushi principle is the mnemonic that minimally processed source data preserves more possible future uses. It does not mean corrupt or undocumented data is automatically valuable.
optionExplanations.d: Designing one complete schema before loading is schema-on-write and resembles a traditional warehouse process. It is the opposite of raw-first collection.

questions.question: Describe the ETL pattern that Hadoop is often used for alongside an MPP data warehouse?

options.text: Raw dumps first, with interpretation deferred to the reader
Hadoop replaces the warehouse entirely, so no ETL is needed
The warehouse performs the ETL and Hadoop stores the results
ETL is performed by the transaction processing systems themselves

questions.explanation: Hadoop commonly receives raw snapshots from OLTP systems, cleans and reshapes them, then loads relational results into an MPP warehouse. Keeping raw bytes in HDFS postpones schema decisions and decouples collection from warehouse modeling.

questions.question: What does 'monolithic' buy an MPP database?

options.text: Monolithic and tightly integrated, tuned for one kind of query
Monolithic design buys flexibility at the cost of performance
Monolithic design buys nothing; it is purely a liability
Monolithic design buys arbitrary code execution

questions.explanation: Tight integration buys tuned performance and analyst-accessible SQL.

questions.question: Why do some batch workloads need a processing model more general than SQL?

options.text: Because not all processing can be expressed as SQL queries
Only reporting workloads need code; everything else fits SQL
SQL can express all these workloads without extension
These workloads require specialized hardware, not code

questions.explanation: Machine learning, relevance ranking, natural-language processing, and image analysis require application-specific algorithms that do not fit naturally into SQL. General batch APIs allow arbitrary code and libraries while the engine handles distributed execution.

questions.question: MPP-style SQL and MapReduce were the two processing models first available on Hadoop. Why were two models not enough?

options.text: Because MapReduce was too limiting and slow for some workloads
Because SQL was too slow and MapReduce too fast
Because two models are always sufficient; no third processing model was ever needed
Because MPP databases already offered every model

questions.explanation: A shared HDFS layer allowed SQL engines, key-value stores, and specialized libraries to operate over the same files. New processing models could be added without copying every dataset into a separate platform.

questions.question: What is the single shared-use cluster argument?

options.text: They all run on one shared cluster over the same files
Each processing model requires its own cluster; HBase and Impala have separate storage
Only MapReduce-based systems can share a cluster
The shared cluster argument applies only to storage, not processing

questions.explanation: A shared HDFS cluster lets several processing models operate over the same files instead of repeatedly importing data into isolated systems. HBase and Impala illustrate this: neither is MapReduce, but both coexist over HDFS.

questions.question: Which two further design differences separate MPP databases from MapReduce?

options.text: Fault handling, and the use of memory versus disk
The choice of query language and the storage format
The network topology and the scheduling policy
The isolation level and the replication factor

questions.explanation: MPP databases typically pipeline operators in memory and may abort or restart a query after a worker failure. MapReduce materializes heavily to disk and retries individual tasks, favoring fault recovery and schedulability over low-latency execution.

questions.question: Describe the environment MapReduce was designed for.

options.text: Mixed-use datacenters, where batch jobs can be preempted
Dedicated batch-only clusters with no priority system at all
Rented cloud virtual machines, which are never preempted
Supercomputers, which checkpoint rather than being preempted

questions.explanation: Individual machines fail infrequently enough that many jobs might finish normally, but shared clusters deliberately preempt low-priority work. Cheap task retry is therefore useful even when hardware is reliable.

questions.question: What hourly preemption risk did Google report for low-priority batch tasks?

options.text: About a 5% risk of being terminated within an hour
A 50% risk per hour, giving near-certain termination for 100 tasks
A 0.5% risk per hour, giving a 5% risk for 100 tasks
A 5% risk per day, giving a 50% risk for 1,000 tasks

questions.explanation: A ten-minute task has a survival probability of roughly 0.95^(1/6), or 99.15%. Across 100 independent tasks, the probability that none is preempted is about 0.9915^100 = 43%, leaving roughly a 57% chance that at least one is killed.

questions.question: What is the real reason MapReduce tolerates frequent termination?

options.text: Because preemption is routine in a mixed-use cluster
Because commodity hardware fails constantly; all open source schedulers preempt
Because networks are unreliable; only Mesos preempts
Because disks wear out; Kubernetes preempts by default

questions.explanation: Frequent task termination is a resource-management choice, not merely a response to unreliable hardware. Mixed-use clusters preempt low-priority batch tasks for online services, and MapReduce's retry model makes that safe; some schedulers support limited queue balancing, though general preemption was historically less common.

questions.question: Why does MapReduce deserve this much attention, and in what sense is it 'simple'?

options.text: One among many possible programming models
Because MapReduce is easy to use and remains the fastest option
Because MapReduce is the only available model
Because MapReduce is simple in both senses of the word

questions.explanation: MapReduce is simple in the sense that user callbacks have narrow contracts while the framework owns placement, shuffle, and retry. It deserves study as a clear baseline, not as the best model for every data volume, structure, or computation.

questions.question: What did Pig, Hive, Cascading, and Crunch improve, and what limitation remained?

options.text: They simplified programming, but MapReduce's execution costs remained
They simplified execution, but mapper and reducer programming stayed unchanged
They removed HDFS materialization, but supported only handwritten callbacks
They added stream processing, but could no longer execute bounded batch jobs

questions.explanation: Pig, Hive, Cascading, and Crunch replaced low-level mapper/reducer plumbing with joins, grouping, filtering, and aggregation. They made jobs easier to express and portable to newer engines, but the original MapReduce engine still paid the cost of repeatedly materializing intermediate state.

questions.question: What does materialization mean in a batch workflow?

options.text: Materialization — eagerly computing and writing intermediate state
Materialization means computing on demand; pipes materialize fully
Both materialize fully; the difference is the storage medium
Each of the two streams its results, so neither materializes anything

questions.explanation: Materialization eagerly computes intermediate results and writes them to storage before the next stage starts. Unix pipes instead stream bounded chunks directly between simultaneously running processes, reducing latency and intermediate I/O.

questions.question: What are the downsides of MapReduce's full materialization? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Stages cannot overlap, and stragglers delay the entire workflow
Redundant mappers often reread freshly materialized reducer output
Temporary intermediate files receive unnecessary distributed replication
Materialized files cannot be reread after a failure

questions.explanation: Materialized files are precisely what makes MapReduce's fault tolerance easy — the trade-off runs the other way.

optionExplanations.a: A downstream MapReduce job cannot start until the upstream job has fully materialized output, so stages cannot pipeline and one straggler holds up the whole workflow.
optionExplanations.b: Every materialized boundary is read again by a new set of mappers, even when the data was just produced. That repeated serialization and disk I/O adds no application value.
optionExplanations.c: HDFS normally replicates intermediate files for durability although many are temporary and cheaply recomputable. Network transfer and storage are spent on data that soon disappears.
optionExplanations.d: Materialization makes intermediate files durable and therefore easy to reread after failure. The downside is excessive I/O and waiting, not loss of recoverability.

questions.question: Name the three best-known dataflow engines?

options.text: Spark, Tez and Flink
Hive, Pig and Cascading, which share a declarative API
HBase, Impala and Drill, which share HDFS storage
Oozie, Azkaban and Airflow, which share a scheduler

questions.explanation: Spark, Tez, and Flink model a complete multi-stage workflow as one dataflow graph. Seeing the whole graph lets the engine pipeline stages, avoid unnecessary sorts and materialization, and recover only the work affected by a failure.

questions.question: Define operator, and give the three ways a dataflow engine can wire one operator's output to another's input. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: An operator is a processing function; a broadcast connection sends one upstream input to every downstream partition
Repartition and sort records by key, enabling grouping and sort-merge joins
Repartition records by key without sorting, which avoids unnecessary work for partitioned hash joins
For broadcast hash joins, the same output from one operator is sent to just one partition of the join operator, chosen by hashing the key

questions.explanation: An operator is a processing function in a flexible dataflow graph. Connections may repartition and sort by key, repartition without sorting, or broadcast one input to every downstream partition; the engine chooses only the data movement each edge requires.

optionExplanations.a: An operator is a processing function in the dataflow graph, and broadcast copies one upstream dataset to every downstream partition. That wiring supports joins with a small shared input.
optionExplanations.b: Repartitioning and sorting by key groups equal keys in order, enabling reduce-style grouping and sort-merge joins. The sort is performed only where that edge requires it.
optionExplanations.c: Hash repartitioning without sorting co-locates equal keys while avoiding unnecessary ordering work. It is appropriate when downstream operators use hash tables rather than ordered groups.
optionExplanations.d: Broadcast sends the relevant small input to every join partition, not to one hashed destination. Sending it once would leave other partitions without the lookup data they need.

questions.question: Which advantages do dataflow engines have over MapReduce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sort and repartition only where a graph edge requires them
Use whole-graph visibility to improve task and data locality
Keep temporary state in memory or local disk instead of replicated HDFS
Wait for an entire upstream stage before starting downstream work

questions.explanation: That is MapReduce's behaviour, not a dataflow engine's. In a dataflow engine an operator starts as soon as its input is ready. Six advantages. You can use dataflow engines to implement the same computations as MapReduce workflows and they usually execute significantly faster — and since operators are a generalization of map and reduce, the same processing code can run on either execution engine: workflows implemented in Pig, Hive or Cascading can be switched from MapReduce to Tez or Spark with a simple configuration change, without modifying code.

optionExplanations.a: A general dataflow graph can leave records in place unless a particular edge needs partitioning or sorting. MapReduce imposes a shuffle boundary for every reduce stage.
optionExplanations.b: Seeing the full operator graph lets the scheduler co-locate dependent work, reuse partitions, and choose better execution order. Separate MapReduce jobs hide those opportunities.
optionExplanations.c: Temporary data can stay in memory or local disk and be regenerated from lineage after failure. It need not be written and replicated through HDFS at every stage.
optionExplanations.d: Waiting for all upstream tasks is the MapReduce materialization barrier. Dataflow operators can normally begin as partitions of their inputs become available.

questions.question: Contrast Tez with Spark and Flink as pieces of software?

options.text: Tez is thin and uses YARN's shuffle service; Spark has its own
Tez is the largest framework; Spark and Flink are thin libraries
All three are thin libraries over YARN
All three ship their own scheduler and network layer

questions.explanation: Tez delegates transport and scheduling to YARN services, whereas Spark and Flink provide more of their own runtime. The trade-off is a thinner integration library versus a larger self-contained engine.
