questions.question: How can dataflow engines recover lost intermediate work without materializing every stage to HDFS?

options.text: Recompute lost work from lineage or restore checkpoints
They replicate intermediate state to three machines, like HDFS
They restart the whole job on any failure
They do not tolerate faults

questions.explanation: Newer engines avoid writing every intermediate result to HDFS. They recover selectively: Spark follows lineage to recompute missing partitions, while Flink restores checkpointed operator state and replays input. The framework's execution graph identifies which work must be repeated.

questions.question: Why does determinism matter when recomputing, and how does nondeterminism creep in? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recomputed output must match data already observed downstream
Hash-table iteration order may vary between executions
Randomized algorithms can produce different results
System-clock reads are identical on every node and execution

questions.explanation: Clock reads and external data sources are nondeterministic, and such causes need to be eliminated before recomputation is safe. Recovering by recomputing data is not always the right answer: if the intermediate data is much smaller than the source data, or if the computation is very CPU-intensive, it is probably cheaper to materialize the intermediate data to files than to recompute it.

optionExplanations.a: Lineage-based recovery is safe only if recomputation reproduces data that downstream operators may already have consumed. Different output could make one logical run internally inconsistent.
optionExplanations.b: Hash-table traversal order may depend on memory layout or runtime details, so the same records can be emitted in a different sequence. Order-sensitive downstream code can then diverge.
optionExplanations.c: Randomized algorithms need controlled seeds or recorded choices to reproduce output. Fresh randomness during recovery can generate a result inconsistent with the original attempt.
optionExplanations.d: System clocks differ across machines and advance between attempts, making clock reads a classic source of nondeterminism. Treating them as identical would invalidate recomputation assumptions.

questions.question: Restate the Unix analogy for materialization?

options.text: MapReduce writes temporary files; dataflow engines are like pipes
Filtering is the blocking operator; sorting can be pipelined
Joining is the blocking operator; sorting can be pipelined
Operators in a dataflow engine never block, which is the key difference from MapReduce

questions.explanation: Sorting is inherently blocking. When the job completes its output needs to go somewhere durable so that users can find it and use it — most likely written to the distributed filesystem again. So with a dataflow engine, materialized datasets on HDFS are still usually the inputs and the final outputs of a job: like with MapReduce the inputs are immutable and the output is completely replaced, and the improvement is that you save writing all the intermediate state to the filesystem. Pipes in the middle, files at the edges.

questions.question: How does whole-graph batch processing differ from OLTP-style graph traversal queries, and what does PageRank compute?

options.text: Batch jobs run algorithms over the whole graph rather than OLTP-style traversals; PageRank ranks a page by what links to it
Batch jobs look up single vertices quickly while OLTP traversals analyse whole graphs; PageRank ranks pages by their size
They are the same use case at two different scales; PageRank simply counts the edges leaving each vertex in the graph
Both walk a few edges out from a chosen starting vertex; PageRank ranks users by how much activity they generate

questions.explanation: OLTP graph queries usually start at selected vertices and follow a small neighborhood. Whole-graph jobs visit the graph at scale; PageRank uses incoming links, weighted by their sources, to estimate importance.

questions.question: Dataflow engines and graph processing both involve graphs. Why is conflating the two a mistake?

options.text: A dataflow engine's graph is a DAG of operators, whereas graph processing analyses graph-structured data
They really are the same thing: a dataflow DAG is just one way of drawing a graph algorithm out
Graph processing needs a cyclic operator graph, which no dataflow engine is able to express at all
Dataflow DAGs cannot express iterative algorithms, so graph algorithms must fall back on MapReduce

questions.explanation: Graph-shaped topology versus graph-shaped data.

questions.question: How are many graph algorithms expressed?

options.text: By traversing one edge at a time, repeatedly
By a single pass over all edges; the example is PageRank
By sorting vertices by degree; the example is clustering
By recursive SQL; the example is a join

questions.explanation: Repeat-until-converged is the shape, and transitive closure is the name of the example.

questions.question: Why does 'repeating until done' break plain MapReduce?

options.text: Repeating until done fits MapReduce badly, as it is not iterative
MapReduce supports iteration natively, so no workaround is needed
The reducer loops internally until convergence
The graph must be processed on a single machine

questions.explanation: Plain MapReduce performs one bounded pass, so iteration lives outside the job. A scheduler runs one step, evaluates whether the graph algorithm has converged, and launches the next step when needed; this works but repeatedly rereads and rewrites the graph.

questions.question: Which graph-processing model lets vertices retain state across synchronized rounds?

options.text: Bulk synchronous parallel (Pregel or vertex-centric)
The MapReduce iteration model, implemented in Oozie
The dataflow model, implemented in Spark and Flink only
The actor model, implemented in Akka

questions.explanation: Bulk synchronous parallel organizes computation into synchronized rounds over stateful vertices and is also called the Pregel or vertex-centric model. Giraph, GraphX, and Gelly implement it, avoiding a full graph rewrite when only some vertices receive messages.

questions.question: How do vertices communicate in the Pregel model?

options.text: A vertex sends messages along its edges to other vertices
Pregel is stateless like MapReduce, but sends messages along edges
Pregel processes all vertices every iteration regardless of activity
Pregel eliminates message passing in favour of shared memory

questions.explanation: A vertex sends messages addressed to neighboring vertex IDs, and the framework delivers them for the next synchronized round. Vertex state persists between rounds, so inactive vertices need not recompute everything.

questions.question: How does Pregel differ from the actor model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Vertex state and messages between vertices are fault-tolerant and durable, and communication is guaranteed
Communication proceeds in fixed rounds: at every iteration the framework delivers all messages sent in the previous iteration, whereas actors normally have no such timing guarantee
Pregel vertices are unable to send messages at all, which is unlike an actor
Pregel vertices carry no state between iterations, which is unlike an actor

questions.explanation: Durability and round-based delivery are the two differences. The fact that vertices can only communicate by message passing, not by querying each other directly, helps improve the performance of Pregel jobs, since messages can be batched and there is less waiting for communication. The only waiting is between iterations: since the model guarantees that all messages sent in one iteration are delivered in the next, the prior iteration must completely finish and all of its messages must be copied over the network before the next one can start. Even though the underlying network may drop, duplicate or arbitrarily delay messages, Pregel implementations guarantee that messages are processed exactly once at their destination vertex in the following iteration.

optionExplanations.a: Pregel checkpoints vertex state and provides reliable delivery semantics across worker failure. Ordinary actor systems often leave durability and message guarantees to the application.
optionExplanations.b: Pregel advances through global supersteps: messages sent in one round become inputs in the next. Actors generally process asynchronously without a framework-wide round boundary.
optionExplanations.c: Pregel vertices communicate by sending messages along graph edges or to vertex IDs. The model restricts direct shared-state access, not messaging itself.
optionExplanations.d: A vertex retains mutable state across supersteps, which is central to iterative graph algorithms. Calling it stateless confuses Pregel with stateless MapReduce callbacks.

questions.question: How does Pregel achieve fault tolerance?

options.text: By checkpointing all vertex state at the end of an iteration
By replicating all vertex state synchronously to three machines
By recomputing from the original input on every failure with no checkpoints
It does not tolerate faults

questions.explanation: Checkpoints for the simple case, determinism plus message logs for selective recovery.

questions.question: What physical-placement information does a vertex know?

options.text: It addresses messages by vertex, not by machine
A vertex must specify the target machine when sending messages
The framework always finds the optimal partitioning
Graphs cannot be partitioned in Pregel

questions.explanation: Thinking like a vertex, with arbitrary partitioning in practice.

questions.question: Given the communication overhead, when should you not use a distributed graph algorithm?

options.text: Heavy cross-machine communication and large intermediate state
Always use a distributed algorithm; single machines are never competitive
Never use a distributed algorithm; graphs always fit on one machine
Use distributed algorithms only for graphs smaller than memory

questions.explanation: Distributed graph processing can move more intermediate messages than the original graph and pay heavy synchronization costs. Prefer an in-memory single-machine algorithm when possible, a disk-based tool such as GraphChi when one host suffices, and Pregel-style distribution only when the graph exceeds one machine.

questions.question: Which storage problem was considered largely solved once HDFS reached very large clusters?

options.text: Reliable distributed storage at enormous scale
Clusters of 100 machines and terabytes; attention turned to hardware
Clusters of 1,000 machines; attention turned to security
Clusters of 100,000 machines; attention turned to networking

questions.explanation: Once HDFS could store and process hundreds of petabytes across more than 10,000 machines reliably, raw physical scale was no longer the central research problem. Work shifted toward friendlier programming models, less I/O, and workloads beyond classic MapReduce.

questions.question: Why did high-level dataflow languages replace handwritten MapReduce jobs?

options.text: Because writing MapReduce jobs by hand is laborious
Because they were faster than raw MapReduce and required no rewrite for SQL
Because they supported streaming from the start
Because they eliminated the need for a cluster

questions.explanation: Relational-style operators remove mapper, reducer, partitioning, and serialization boilerplate. Because those operators describe a dataflow rather than one engine, the same job can later run on Tez, Spark, or Flink.

questions.question: Beyond less code, what advantage do high-level interfaces bring?

options.text: Interactive incremental development in a shell
They eliminate the need for a cluster
They guarantee exactly-once semantics
They provide low-latency query responses

questions.explanation: An interactive shell shortens the edit-run-inspect loop, while the compiler or optimizer translates the high-level dataflow into efficient machine-level operators. The user gets rapid iteration without giving up execution efficiency.

questions.question: What does a cost-based optimizer do for joins?

options.text: Because declared joins let the optimizer choose the algorithm
It rewrites the user-defined functions for greater speed
It chooses only the number of reducers to allocate
Cost-based optimization is absent from every batch processing framework

questions.explanation: Declarative specification is what makes automatic algorithm selection possible.

questions.question: How do MapReduce and its successors differ from SQL's fully declarative model?

options.text: Around callbacks, not around declarative queries
They are fully declarative and cannot run arbitrary code
They use a restricted expression language with no callbacks
They differ only in syntax

questions.explanation: The freedom to easily run arbitrary code is what has long distinguished batch processing systems of MapReduce heritage from MPP databases. Although databases have facilities for writing user-defined functions, they are often cumbersome to use and not well integrated with the package managers and dependency management systems that are widely used in most programming languages — such as Maven for Java, npm for JavaScript and Rubygems for Ruby.

questions.question: Why does even a trivial filter benefit from being declared, and what optimizations does that unlock? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because if a callback function contains only a simple filtering condition, or it just selects some fields from a record, then there is significant CPU overhead in calling the function on every record

Columnar reads: if such simple filtering and mapping operations are expressed in a declarative way, the query optimizer can take advantage of column-oriented storage layouts and read only the required columns from disk
Vectorized execution: Hive, Spark DataFrames and Impala use vectorized execution, iterating over data in a tight inner loop that is friendly to CPU caches and avoiding function calls
Code generation is deliberately avoided in these engines, since interpreting the callback directly turns out to be faster

questions.explanation: Both do generate code: Spark emits JVM bytecode and Impala uses LLVM to produce native code for the inner loops. By incorporating declarative aspects in their high-level APIs, and having query optimizers that can take advantage of them during execution, batch processing frameworks begin to look more like MPP databases and can achieve comparable performance — while by retaining the extensibility of being able to run arbitrary code and read data in arbitrary formats, they keep their flexibility advantage. As batch processing systems gain built-in functionality and high-level declarative operators, and as MPP databases become more programmable and flexible, the two are beginning to look more alike: in the end, they are all just systems for storing and processing data.

optionExplanations.a: Calling a general-purpose callback for every record adds dispatch, boxing, and interpretation overhead even when the operation is a trivial predicate or projection.
optionExplanations.b: A declarative list of required fields lets the optimizer read only those columns from columnar storage. Opaque callback code hides that information and forces broader reads.
optionExplanations.c: Vectorized execution processes batches in tight cache-friendly loops rather than crossing a function boundary for every row. This improves CPU efficiency for simple operators.
optionExplanations.d: Spark and Impala can generate JVM bytecode or native code for hot loops. Claiming code generation is deliberately avoided reverses an important optimization.

questions.question: Why is extensibility not enough on its own?

options.text: Because standard processing patterns keep recurring
Extensibility is sufficient; no reusable libraries exist
Only Mahout exists, for machine learning
Reusable libraries exist only inside MPP databases

questions.explanation: Arbitrary callbacks provide extensibility, but recurring algorithms are better supplied as tested building blocks. Examples include Mahout and MADlib for machine learning, k-nearest neighbors for similarity search, and approximate string matching for genomics.

questions.question: Which design principles did MapReduce and the dataflow engines inherit from Unix?

options.text: Immutable inputs, output as another program's input, and composition
That programs should be monolithic, typed and interactive
That data should be modeled up front and validated on write
That outputs should be mutable and reused in place

questions.explanation: Note the parenthetical 'as yet unknown' — the program consuming your output may not exist yet.

questions.question: In the Unix-style layered model of distributed batch processing, what uniform interface is presented between programs and at the system boundaries?

options.text: Files and pipes in Unix; a distributed filesystem in MapReduce
Unix uses pipes only; MapReduce uses pipes; dataflow engines use files
All three use the same distributed filesystem
Dataflow engines have no uniform interface

questions.explanation: Distributed files hold durable job inputs and outputs; engine-managed pipes move temporary data between operators. The separation keeps program logic independent from cluster wiring and recovery.

questions.question: Which two responsibilities must every distributed batch framework handle?

options.text: Partitioning work and recovering from faults
Replication and compression, solved identically by both
Scheduling and monitoring, solved by YARN in both cases
Encoding and serialization, solved by Avro in both cases

questions.explanation: MapReduce derives map partitions from input blocks, hashes mapper output into reducer partitions, and relies on durable intermediate files for retry. Newer engines choose repartitioning only where a graph edge needs it and recover through lineage, checkpoints, or selective recomputation.

questions.question: Describe the three join algorithms available to a batch processor. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sort-merge: repartition and sort both inputs by join key
Broadcast hash: load a small input into every mapper
Partitioned hash: join buckets that use identical partitioning
These algorithms have no counterpart in parallel databases

questions.explanation: Sort-merge joins repartition and order both sides, broadcast hash joins replicate a small side, and partitioned hash joins exploit matching buckets. Parallel databases use the same underlying algorithms.

optionExplanations.a: A sort-merge join repartitions both inputs by key and sorts each partition so matching groups can be streamed together. It handles large inputs at the cost of shuffle and sort.
optionExplanations.b: A broadcast hash join builds a hash table from a sufficiently small input on every mapper or partition. The large input then streams locally without repartitioning.
optionExplanations.c: A partitioned hash join reuses identical bucket boundaries on both inputs, allowing corresponding buckets to join locally. Mismatched partitioning would require another shuffle.
optionExplanations.d: Parallel databases use the same underlying sort-merge and hash-join families. The execution frameworks differ, but the relational algorithms are not unique to batch processors.

questions.question: What restriction makes callback functions safe to retry?

options.text: Callbacks must be stateless and have no externally visible side effects
Callbacks may be stateful and have side effects, which the framework tracks
The restriction buys only performance, not fault tolerance
Callbacks may do anything at all, since the framework imposes no restriction

questions.explanation: A framework may invoke a callback again after failure. If the callback keeps hidden mutable state or performs an external side effect, retry can produce a different result or duplicate an action. Stateless, side-effect-free callbacks can be recomputed deterministically.

questions.question: What is the defining property of a batch processing job?

options.text: That it reads input and produces output without modifying the input
That it achieves the lowest possible latency for each individual record
That it keeps both its input and its output inside HDFS specifically
That it always takes the shape of one map step and one reduce step

questions.explanation: Bounded input is what makes completion meaningful — and losing it is what makes stream processing different.
